# The server was part of the appliance

A connected appliance is two machines sold as one. One machine sits in your house, draws power from your wall, and belongs to you. The other sits in a data center, obeys the vendor, and may disappear when the vendor loses interest. The box remains on your shelf, but part of the appliance has been repossessed.

When a vendor closes its cloud service, the failure can look strangely selective. The switch may still switch. The camera may still capture an image. The thermostat may still measure temperature. But the app can't log in, schedules won't update, remote controls don't respond, notifications vanish, voice integrations break, and devices that once coordinated become isolated boxes. You haven't worn out the product. Someone else has turned off the half that lived elsewhere (the half you couldn't see).

What, exactly, did you buy? The receipt probably described a camera, lock, light, speaker, hub, or kitchen appliance. Yet the useful thing was a chain: sensor, software, account, server, and command sent back to your home. Remove the server and the chain breaks – not because your hardware failed, but because the vendor retained a critical link after taking your money.

That changes the original bargain. A sale ordinarily means that the seller gives up control while the buyer gains it. Cloud-dependent hardware reverses that transfer (quietly, and often completely). You get possession; the vendor keeps the power to decide whether essential functions continue. I call that a sale with a tenancy hidden inside it. You've bought the walls, but somebody else still owns the boiler room.

Of course, servers cost money, security work continues, and no online service can be promised forever. But “forever” isn't the standard. The question is whether foreseeable shutdown was designed as an inconvenience or as a product death. If the company can end service without releasing a local path, then it hasn't merely stopped providing an extra. It's reached into your house and subtracted capability from an appliance you already paid for – a remarkable privilege for any seller to reserve.

I don't need every connected feature to survive unchanged. I do expect the ordinary functions to outlive the vendor's enthusiasm. I can accept losing an optional remote dashboard more readily than losing schedules, automations, recordings, access codes, or the ability to pair replacement sensors. The distinction is simple (and useful): features that inherently require an outside network may expire; features your hardware can perform at home should remain available at home.

Local operation protects that boundary. A local interface lets your phone talk directly to the device. Local accounts keep authentication inside the household. Exportable keys and documented protocols let another controller take over. On-device schedules keep running when the internet fails. A local hub can preserve automations among devices even after the original app goes dark. None of this guarantees eternal support, but it prevents one server shutdown from becoming a remote demolition crew.

There is a familiar market analogy here. Imagine buying a washing machine whose start button sends a request to the manufacturer. The manufacturer checks your account, approves the cycle, and tells the motor to turn. Years later it closes that department, so the drum and pump remain perfectly sound while the machine becomes a large metal cupboard. We'd recognize the arrangement as absurd – connected software merely makes the same damn trick easier to hide.

So inspect the failure mode before you buy. Can you control the device without an account? Are schedules stored locally? Can you export data, replace the controller, or install independent software? A vendor may call local operation an advanced feature (or leave it out of the brochure), but for owners it is the difference between resilience and permission.

We should demand products that fail gently. We can tolerate a remote service ending; we shouldn't accept the destruction of local utility as its automatic consequence. Our devices live in our homes, shape our routines, and consume our money. The server was part of the appliance. If that server can vanish, the appliance needs a local way to remain yours.
